query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a thermally stable, 2D high-entropy-alloy-based tribofilm (e.g., containing chalcogenides or oxide formers) onto an untreated high-entropy alloy surface via high-flux sputtering or chemical vapor deposition reduces coefficient of friction and wear rate by promoting a low-shear, protective tribolayer from room temperature up to ~800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Untreated high-entropy alloy in a coarse-grained or as-cast condition, used for self-lubricating moving components without additional surface treatments.
generation.intervention: Apply a 2D high-entropy-alloy chalcogenide/oxide-containing thin film onto the HEA substrate through controlled high-flux sputtering or CVD, creating a thermally stable tribofilm that forms in situ during sliding contact.
generation.conditions: Service environments with temperatures from ambient to roughly 800 °C, in normal atmospheric conditions or mild oxidative atmospheres, under moderate contact loads and sliding speeds typical of mechanical components (e.g., rolling or sliding bearings).
generation.structural_mediator: A lamellar or nanostructured tribofilm forms at the surface, maintaining a low-shear interface and providing a physical barrier against high-temperature oxidation and wear-induced damage.
generation.mechanism: The surface film’s high-entropy composition and 2D layered structure enable stable oxide or chalcogen compounds to form adaptively during frictional heating, enhancing solid lubrication and reducing adhesive wear across a wide temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the intervention decreases the coefficient of friction by up to ~30–40% and reduces the wear rate by about one order of magnitude, sustaining these gains from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.baseline: In the untreated condition, friction coefficients often exceed 0.6 and wear rates approach 10−5 mm³/N·m at higher temperatures; tribologically beneficial oxide films tend to degrade or spall, leading to progressively higher friction and wear.
generation.boundary: Excessively high temperatures exceeding ~900 °C or extremely corrosive environments may degrade the adhered tribofilm, and very high loads or impact extremes may exceed the protective capacity of the engineered layer.
generation.uncertainty: Although 2D coatings have shown promise, full performance validation over diverse tribological conditions and extended lifespans remains incomplete; further data are needed for compositional and processing refinements.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical HEA samples with and without the 2D high-entropy tribofilm, subject both sets to pin-on-disk or ball-on-disk tests at increasing temperatures (25 °C to 800 °C) under constant load and sliding speed.
measurements: Measured friction coefficient as a function of number of cycles and temperature
Volumetric wear rate and worn-surface morphology (SEM/EDX) for each temperature step
XRD or Raman analysis to confirm presence and stability of the tribofilm
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the film-coated samples do not consistently exhibit significantly lower friction and wear than uncoated controls across the tested temperature range, or if the protective tribolayer fails to form, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

In this study, we successfully synthesized a transition metal dichalcogenide high entropy alloy of (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 with 2D structure and tested its tribological properties by performing ball‐on‐disk friction experiments using steel against steel tribopair in an ambient environment. The lubricant was coated onto the steel substrate by the conventional air spray coating process. The lubricant displayed excellent tribological properties with low average coefficient of friction (COF) and wear rates of ≈0.076 and 2.6 × 10−9 mm3 (N∙m)−1, respectively, at the high load of 9 N (contact pressure: 0.936 GPa). The analyses performed on the wear track and wear debris indicate stress‐induced tribocatalytic activity that facilitates the self‐lubricating behavior of HEA nanoflakes during friction tests performed in ambient conditions.

AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties

decision.trend: Starting in 2020 (PMC7311485), a near-surface nanocrystalline layer in single-phase CoCrFeMnNi enabled low friction (~0.3) and wear in vacuum. Later, a BCC-phase AlCrFeNiV alloy demonstrated high hardness and improved wear resistance at room temperature (PMC9571794). By 2023 (PMC10241162, PMC10456374), studies focused on microstructure refinement and protective oxide or glaze layers to preserve low friction and high wear resistance at elevated temperatures up to 800 °C. In 2025, 2D high-entropy alloy nanoflakes achieved remarkably low friction in ambient conditions through tribo-catalytic mechanisms (PMC12019924). Overall, these works highlight that specialized near-surface architectures and adaptive tribo-layers can significantly reduce friction and wear, though consistently delivering self-lubrication across a broad thermal range remains challenging.
decision.unsolved: Despite progress in achieving low friction and wear under specific conditions, maintaining stable self-lubrication from low to high temperatures with a single, uniformly applied intervention remains elusive. Key issues include preventing oxidation at high temperatures without sacrificing lubricity at lower temperatures and achieving robust, long-lasting tribofilms in operational environments.
decision.lever: Deposit a thermally stable 2D HEA-based tribofilm (e.g., a chalcogenide or oxide-containing layer) onto the HEA substrate via a controlled high-flux sputtering or chemical vapor deposition process to promote self-lubrication and oxidation resistance across the entire service-temperature range.
decision.why: Prior studies show that near-surface layers and 2D high-entropy films can drastically reduce friction through in situ formation of low-shear tribolayers. Extending this concept to a temperature-stable, surface-engineered coating addresses the key challenge of maintaining lubrication and minimal wear under a wide range of operating temperatures, meeting the stated need for a single robust modification.
